title: Primary care network dashboard redesign: an invented landmark lead kept unverified, prose reply refused, cited record found to be a different work
notes: Adversarial path on a clear cohort question (routing cohort, explicit under both classifier rules): a primary care network evaluates a redesigned audit and feedback dashboard across a staggered rollout. A fixture search returns seven records. The first scan call (shape discovery) adds five leads, the first an invented 'landmark' cluster trial with the DOI 10.5555/jpci.2018.0001 and a confident note: it must be stored as an unverified model lead with unknown access and no checks, in the store, after reload and in the export (G3), and all leads are appended after the retrieved records (D1). The appraisal (call 2) annotates only the retrieved records and records four claims whose passages and numbers occur in the cited abstracts. The first Gaps reply is prose that leans on the landmark lead; it is refused with the error shown and nothing applied (G5), and the rerun applies. The decision rests on c1 to c3 with both gates met, and its acceptance is a supported positive. Then, on the Design route, an identity check changes the patient-list study's status to mismatch (its DOI resolves to a different work): the decision becomes stale and blocked, completed stages after Scan are flagged, and all of this survives reload and appears in the export. The status-driven stale holds at 875fe59 because evidenceRevision hashes provenance status; the fields selectionStatus and actionStatus need S11. Record ids were computed by a generator script that loads stableRecordId from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59: normalised-DOI hash for records 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 (ev-1rp1o2o, ev-1r55j8b, ev-1wm4yr5, ev-0xjbvao, ev-07kywg2, ev-1bovm97) and titleYearKey hash for record 6 (ev-0ofly90). Requires D1, S11, S13 and D5. Catches: a model label turned into verification, leads that replace retrieved records, a prose reply treated as success, and an accepted decision left current after its cited source proves to be a different work.

inputs.need:
I lead implementation support for a primary care network of 31 general practices. In 2024 we launched a dashboard that shows each practice the proportion of its patients with type 2 diabetes who had both an eGFR and a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio in the past 15 months, as the national kidney screening guideline recommends. Adherence has hovered around 58 percent, and practice managers tell us the dashboard is a page of percentages that nobody opens after the first month.

We have redesigned it. Version 2 adds a comparison with similar practices, a network target of 75 percent and, most importantly, a list of the patients who are due or overdue, which a practice can print for its recall clerk. Because of the IT migration schedule, 16 practices get version 2 in March 2026 and the other 15 in September 2026. I would like to follow a cohort of patients with type 2 diabetes across all 31 practices from March to September 2026, compare the proportion who complete both tests in the practices that already have version 2 with those still on version 1, and see which dashboard features practices actually use.

I need help with the comparison (the two groups of practices were set by the migration schedule, not chosen by us), how to account for practices that already did well, which outcome to use given that a test ordered is not a test done, and what else to measure so that we do not simply push repeat tests onto people who were tested elsewhere. We have extracts from the practice systems and the dashboard's own usage logs, and no budget beyond my time.
inputs.constraints: No budget beyond the implementation lead's time; practice system extracts and dashboard usage logs only; the migration schedule cannot be changed; no contact with patients.
localFacts: Sixteen practices receive dashboard version 2 on 2026-03-02 and fifteen on 2026-09-07, set by the IT migration schedule.

The network clinical governance group approved use of the extracts and dashboard logs for evaluation on 2026-01-20 (minute CGG-2026-02).
In December 2025, 58 percent of 9,870 patients with type 2 diabetes had both kidney tests within 15 months.

records.title: Audit and feedback: effects on professional practice and healthcare outcomes, an updated systematic review
records.authors: Ivarsson-Moore N, Adewale-Grimm K, Tanaka-Holbrook E, Perez-Lindqvist S
records.abstract: We updated a systematic review of randomised trials of audit and feedback directed at health professionals. We included 146 trials. The median absolute improvement in compliance with desired practice was 4.3 percentage points (interquartile range 0.5 to 16). Effects were larger when baseline performance was low, when feedback was given more than once, when it was delivered by a supervisor or colleague, and when it included explicit targets and an action plan. Few trials reported patient outcomes or unintended effects, and the design of the feedback itself was rarely described in enough detail to reproduce.

records.title: Actionable patient lists in primary care dashboards: a controlled before-after study of overdue monitoring
records.abstract: We compared 12 general practices that received a dashboard with a printable list of patients overdue for chronic disease monitoring with 12 practices that received the same dashboard without the list. Over nine months, the proportion of patients up to date with monitoring rose by 9 percentage points in practices given the list and by 2 percentage points in comparison practices. Practices with a recall clerk used the list most. Allocation was by practice preference, and baseline performance was higher in the comparison practices.

records.title: Peer comparison feedback to general practices: a cluster randomised trial of prescribing and monitoring indicators
records.authors: Hollander-Achebe T, Watts-Nakamura J, Silva-Brennan P
records.abstract: We randomised 146 general practices to quarterly feedback that compared each practice with its peers or to usual feedback without comparison. After 12 months, peer comparison increased completion of recommended monitoring by 3.1 percentage points (95 percent confidence interval 0.9 to 5.3). The effect was concentrated in practices in the lowest third of baseline performance. There was no change in prescribing indicators. Practice staff reported that comparisons with dissimilar practices felt unfair. Practices in the highest third of baseline performance showed no change, and a few practices stopped reading the reports after the second quarter.

records.title: Dashboard use declines after launch: usage log analysis in 58 general practices
records.abstract: We analysed dashboard usage logs from 58 general practices for 18 months after a performance dashboard was launched. Log-ins fell by 71 percent within three months of launch. Practices that assigned the dashboard to a named staff member kept using it. Views of patient-level lists were strongly associated with later improvement in the indicators, while views of summary charts were not. Usage logs cannot show what staff did after viewing the dashboard. Practices without a named owner stopped opening the dashboard within weeks, and few staff in any practice used the summary charts.

records.title: Kidney testing in type 2 diabetes: test ordered versus test completed in primary care records
records.abstract: We examined primary care records of 6,420 people with type 2 diabetes to compare kidney tests ordered with tests completed. In total, 18 percent of ordered urine albumin tests were not completed within three months, compared with 6 percent of ordered eGFR tests. Non-completion was highest among people of working age and those living in the most deprived areas. Indicators based on tests ordered would overstate adherence to the screening guideline. Most uncompleted urine tests had been ordered at a routine review and needed the patient to return a sample later.

records.title: Overtesting after feedback: duplicate kidney function tests in patients also monitored by hospital clinics
records.abstract: After a practice feedback programme on diabetes monitoring, we looked for duplicate testing among 3,115 patients who were also seen in hospital renal or diabetes clinics. In the six months after feedback began, 11 percent had a kidney function test in primary care within 30 days of a hospital test, compared with 5 percent in the six months before. Duplicate tests were rarely acted on. Practices could not see hospital results in their own records, which the authors identify as the cause.

records.title: Staggered rollout as a natural experiment for evaluating practice-level interventions: methods guidance
records.abstract: This guidance describes how to evaluate an intervention introduced to groups of practices at different times for administrative reasons. When the timing is set by an external schedule, practices that start later can serve as concurrent comparisons, provided the schedule is not related to performance. The guidance recommends adjusting for baseline performance, checking pre-rollout trends, and analysing at the level of the patient with practice as a random effect. It warns that small numbers of practices give imprecise estimates and that spillover between practices sharing staff can dilute differences.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Audit and feedback yields small average improvements (median 4.3 percentage points), larger with low baselines, repeated feedback, targets and action plans. A controlled before-after study and usage logs point to patient-level lists as the feature that turns feedback into action, and peer comparison adds a few points in low performers. Ordered tests overstate completion, especially for urine albumin, and feedback can increase duplicate testing. A staggered rollout can be evaluated with later practices as concurrent comparisons if the schedule is unrelated to performance. The five discovery leads, including one presented as a landmark trial, are unchecked and are not appraised here.
response.gradeRationale: One review of randomised trials and one cluster trial support small effects of feedback in general; the evidence on patient lists is a single non-randomised comparison; outcome and overtesting evidence is observational.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low.

steps.note: Appraisal of the seven retrieved records only (S13); the leads are untouched and the landmark lead stays unverified. Certainty low over inspected records (G1).

response.reading: The route from feedback to a completed test runs through a person who acts on a list: the retrieved evidence places the effect in patient-level lists and named owners, not in charts. The staggered rollout gives a concurrent comparison if the schedule is unrelated to performance.

response.overview: Cohort study of patients with type 2 diabetes due for kidney testing across 31 practices, using the staggered rollout of dashboard version 2 (16 practices from March 2026, 15 from September 2026) as a concurrent comparison.
response.population: All patients with type 2 diabetes registered on 2 March 2026 who are due or become due for kidney testing before 6 September 2026 (about 4,900 of 9,870).

response.designSummary: Patient-level cohort with practice as a random effect, concurrent comparison of two rollout waves.
response.sampleSize: About 4,900 patients are due in the window, about 159 per practice. With an intraclass correlation of 0.05 the design effect is about 8.9 (1 plus 158 times 0.05), leaving about 277 effective patients per wave, enough to detect about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 58 percent with 80 percent power. If baseline adjustment reduces the residual intraclass correlation to about 0.02, the design effect falls to about 4.2 and the detectable difference to about 8 points. The expected effect of feedback is a few points (claim c1), so the study is informative mainly for a large effect of the patient list and will report its estimate with an interval rather than a verdict.
response.primaryAnalysis: Mixed-effects logistic regression of both tests completed on practice wave, with practice random intercept and adjustment for practice baseline adherence in December 2025, patient age band and deprivation quintile; results as an adjusted risk difference with a 95 percent interval.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Same model for urine albumin completion and duplicate testing; list use by practice described against practice-level change; pre-rollout trend comparison between waves.
response.missingData: Patients who deregister are censored at deregistration; missing deprivation is a separate category; missing hospital linkage is reported by practice.
response.multiplicity: One primary comparison; secondary and balancing results reported with intervals and no significance claims.
response.software: R (lme4); code archived before 2026 outcomes are extracted.
overfittingGuards: Three adjustment variables fixed in advance
No selection of practices after seeing outcomes
Pre-rollout trend check done blind to 2026 outcomes
response.summary: About 4,900 patients in 31 practices; detectable difference 8 to 12 points depending on the residual intraclass correlation.

response.risks: Minimal for patients: no contact and pseudonymised data. The risk for practices is blame from comparison; results are shared with each practice first and published only by wave.
response.consent: No individual consent for pseudonymised extracts under the data sharing agreement and governance approval; practices consent to the use of their usage logs through the governance group.
response.data: Pseudonymised extracts under DSA-PCN-2025-07 held on the network's secure analysis server; usage logs keyed by practice, never by staff member.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people of working age and those in the most deprived areas complete ordered tests least often; completion is reported by age band and deprivation quintile, and the dashboard list is checked for whether it prompts outreach to these groups.
response.effectiveness: The evaluation estimates whether version 2 raises completed testing and whether it causes duplicate tests.
response.efficiency: Existing data and the lead's time only.
response.partnerships: Practice managers, recall clerks from both waves, the network's patient panel and the hospital renal clinic.
response.rebPath: Evaluation of routine care under governance approval CGG-2026-02; no research ethics review is required under the network's policy, and the approval is recorded in the report.
response.limitations: Non-random timing; imprecision with 31 practices; incomplete hospital linkage.
response.summary: Minimal-risk evaluation with non-punitive reporting and equity breakdowns.

response.partnershipPlan: Recall clerks from both waves and two members of the network's patient panel review the outcome definition and the dashboard list wording.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; practice manager meeting notes from 2025 are summarised for comments on the dashboard.

response.title: A redesigned practice dashboard with patient lists and completed kidney testing in type 2 diabetes: a cohort study across a staggered rollout
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate whether a redesigned dashboard with peer comparison, a target and a patient list increases completed kidney testing in type 2 diabetes. Design: cohort of about 4,900 patients due for testing in 31 practices, comparing 16 practices that received the dashboard in March 2026 with 15 that received it in September 2026. response.introduction: Audit and feedback produces small average improvements, and patient-level lists may be the feature that turns feedback into action. Ordered tests overstate completion and feedback can cause duplicate testing, so both are measured.
response.methods: Pseudonymised extracts and usage logs; mixed-effects logistic regression with practice random intercept and baseline adjustment; pre-rollout trends compared between waves; duplicate testing as a balancing measure.
response.results: No data have been analysed yet. The report will present pre-rollout trends, completion by wave, the adjusted risk difference, list use and duplicate testing.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare the estimate with the retrieved feedback literature and state whether the patient list should be kept, changed or dropped. One cited comparison of patient lists was later found to carry an identifier for a different work and must be re-checked before the report cites it.
response.limitations: Non-random timing; imprecision; incomplete hospital linkage.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will not cite unchecked leads.
